pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: In your Task struct, what do `json:"notes,omitempty"` and `json:"-"` each do? And why would a lowercase field like `auditToken` never appear in the JSON even without any tag?
expected_points: the tag renames the field's JSON key; omitempty drops the field when it holds the type's zero value
json:"-" excludes an exported field from encoding entirely
unexported fields are invisible to encoding/json because packages can only see exported identifiers — they are skipped silently, not by choice

questions.prompt: You unmarshal a JSON document into a Task. The document contains a field your struct doesn't have, and is missing a field your struct does have. What happens in each case?
expected_points: unknown JSON fields are ignored without error — the sender can add fields without breaking you
missing fields are left untouched: zero value in a fresh struct, existing data preserved in a reused one
nothing signals that a field was absent, which is exactly the gap pointer fields fill

questions.prompt: How did encoding/json know to call your Priority's MarshalJSON — you never registered it anywhere. And why must UnmarshalJSON be on the pointer receiver?
expected_points: Priority satisfies json.Marshaler implicitly — the encoder checks the interface, same mechanism as io.Reader
MarshalJSON must return valid JSON bytes, hence delegating to json.Marshal for correct quoting
UnmarshalJSON mutates the receiver, so it needs the pointer; only *Priority's method set satisfies json.Unmarshaler

questions.prompt: In TaskPatch you used *string for Title instead of string. What concrete pair of inputs would ApplyPatch get wrong with a plain string, and when is a plain value with omitempty the better choice?
expected_points: {"title":""} and {} both leave a plain string as "" — clear-the-title and don't-touch-it become indistinguishable
nil pointer means absent, non-nil means present, even pointing at the zero value
prefer a plain value when zero and absent genuinely mean the same thing; reach for the pointer only when the program must act differently on absent vs zero

questions.prompt: What do json.Encoder and json.Decoder buy you over Marshal/Unmarshal plus io.ReadAll, and how does your ReadTasks loop know the difference between a finished stream and a broken one?
expected_points: they work incrementally against io.Writer/io.Reader, so memory doesn't scale with stream size and callers compose (bytes.Buffer in tests, files or network in production)
Encode writes one value plus a newline — a loop naturally produces NDJSON; Decode reads one value per call
io.EOF at a value boundary (checked with errors.Is) is the clean end; any other error, like io.ErrUnexpectedEOF mid-value, is a real failure

questions.prompt: A teammate adds omitempty to the Done field: `json:"done,omitempty"`. All tests they wrote still pass. What did they just break?
expected_points: every Done=false task now marshals without a done key at all — false is the zero value
consumers can no longer tell 'not done' from 'field absent'; the document's meaning changed
omitempty is only safe when zero and absent are genuinely synonymous

questions.prompt: You decode `{"count": 3}` into a map[string]any and assert the value with .(int). The assertion fails. Why, and what does this suggest about decoding into typed structs?
expected_points: JSON has no integer type, so numbers decode into any as float64
the assertion needs .(float64) — or better, avoid the situation
a typed struct is a schema: declaring Count int makes the decoder do the conversion and the checking for you
